schools.summary: Ellicott: the poet's private feeling is here first swallowed up in a human sense of God's relation to all mankind; 'excellent' is LXX/Vulg. 'wonderful,' better 'great'; the clause 'who hast set thy glory' is corrupt, Ewald's 'thy splendour raised above the heavens' preferred.

Clarke reports the title 'concerning the wine-presses' (a vintage psalm) and the Chaldee 'harp brought out of Gath,' and parses Adonai (root dan, to rule/support) as our Prop and Stay; Wesley: the name now in all nations shows the psalm speaks of the Messiah.

Calvin leaves Gittith undecided (instrument, tune, or song) but rejects 'city of Gath,' and takes the 'name' as the knowledge of God's perfections, not his essence; Gill owns him the one God, Lord of angels and men, King of saints.
Henry records Hammond's conjecture that Gittith = 'the Gittite' (Goliath), doubting it since Ps. 81 and 84 share the title, and presses the possessive 'our Lord' — ours because he made and keeps us.
Augustine reads the wine-press of the title, like the threshing-floor, as the Church, where good and bad are for a time separated in affection, as corn from chaff and wine from husks.

debates.question: What does the title 'upon Gittith' mean?

sides.position: a musical instrument, tune, or well-known song
'upon the Gittite' — Goliath of Gath, the enemy stilled by a stripling
'concerning the wine-presses' — a psalm for the vintage
'the harp David brought out of Gath'

outliers.note: Allegorizes the wine-press of the title as the Church, in which the good are separated from the bad in affection — a spiritual reading of the superscription rather than a lexical one.

themes: the name in all the earth

schools.summary: Ellicott weighs 'perfected praise' (LXX, quoted Matt. 21:16, strength = homage) against 'strength' as a stronghold/defence demanded by the martial context (Ewald), and reads a child's unspoilt wonder as proof of man's likeness to God.
Gill refuses the literal infants of the Jewish writers and reads the babes figuratively of the apostles and first preachers of the gospel, babes in their own and the world's eyes.

Clarke finds the first fulfilment in the temple children's 'Hosanna,' the enemy and avenger being the chief priests and scribes, and dwells on the pneumatic wonder of the nursing infant as the finger of God.

Henry gathers the three kingdoms — nature (helpless children), providence (weak instruments), grace (the apostles who threw down the devil's kingdom); Spurgeon: children's testimony refutes the atheist, as the temple 'Hosanna' silenced the Pharisees.

sides.position: literal infants — the wonder of a nursing child
holders: the Jewish writers (as reported by Gill)

sides.position: figuratively the apostles and gospel-preachers, and the children who cried Hosanna
'strength' — a stronghold or defence, as the martial context demands
'perfected praise' — the LXX reading our Lord quotes at Matt. 21:16

outliers.note: Turns aside into a long physical demonstration of how an infant exhausts its mouth of air to suck, calling the 'pure Boylean vacuum' it makes the finger of God and an argument to still every atheist.

themes: out of the mouth of babes

schools.summary: Henry sets the meditation on a moonlit night-walk and draws dignity from man's erect, upward gaze, making the survey a preface to wonder at God's condescension; Spurgeon: a survey of the heavens abases the pride of puny man.
Clarke makes the omission of the sun deliberate art (it would eclipse the moon and stars), heaps up the magnitudes of the planets, and against Horsley and Kennicott insists the text needs no mending.

Keil and Delitzsch: the silence about the sun proves a night hymn, and this verse is the protasis whose principal clause is v.4's question; Ellicott glosses 'consider' as 'scan' and 'ordained' as 'founded,' welcoming the note of order.

debates.question: Why does the psalm name the moon and stars but not the sun?

sides.position: a deliberate omission — a night scene and a poetic design that lets the lesser lights show
the text is defective and the sun should be restored
holders: Horsley and Kennicott (as reported by Clarke)

themes: moon and stars, not the sun

schools.summary: Gill reads 'man' exclusively of the man Christ Jesus — Enosh the frail worm and man of sorrows subject to death — not Adam in innocence nor his posterity, since all things are not put under them.

Ellicott takes it of man as man, between frailty and glory (Pascal), against the modern poet's 'sad astrology'; Keil and Delitzsch read a real man, a king soon given a kingdom, the NT application noted.
Henry takes the verse of both at once — first of mankind in general, the worm yet the darling of Providence, then 'in a particular manner' of Jesus Christ (Heb. 2:6-8).
Clarke keeps it, for now, upon fallen man 'full of infirmity, ignorance, and sin,' reading God's 'visiting' as the Spirit convincing of sin and keeping man salvable.

debates.question: Is the 'man' God is mindful of the literal son of Adam or the man Christ Jesus?

sides.position: exclusively the Messiah — the man Christ Jesus, of whom alone the high words are strictly true
man as man, the literal creature between frailty and glory (the psalm's own sense)
both — the literal sense fulfilled and transcended in Christ (Heb. 2)
fallen man visited by the Spirit, rising to Christ in the sequel

schools.summary: Gill reads Elohim as 'than God,' referring the verse to the human nature of Christ made a little lower than God in its near union with the Son.
Clarke renders 'thou hast lessened him for a little time from God,' a temporal abasement, referring the reader to his notes on Heb. 2:6.

Ellicott: Elohim can include angels and God, but nothing limits it to angels; the sense is 'want but a little from God,' little less than Divine, the AV following the LXX to tone down a too-bold expression.
Spurgeon hears 'a little while' — man lowered by the suffering of death and in Christ raised above the immortal angels; Henry finds man's crown of glory in his reason and rule.

debates.question: Is 'a little lower than Elohim' lower than God or lower than the angels?

sides.position: than God — the grammatical sense, referring to Christ's human nature
than the angels — the LXX/AV reading adopted by Hebrews, a toning-down
holders: the Septuagint and Hebrews (as reported by Ellicott)

debates.question: Does 'a little' measure degree or time?

sides.position: a little in degree — 'little less than Divine'
a little while in time — lowered for a season, then exalted

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch make 'put under his feet' a paraphrase of the dominion of Gen. 1:26 — man a king with a territory, the unlimited 'all' narrowed by the psalm to land, air, and sea; Ellicott keeps the survey of animated nature and points to Paul's elevation of it (1 Cor. 15:27).
Henry dates man's charter from creation and its renewal after the flood (Gen. 9:2), holds both senses, and finds in Christ's stilling of winds and seas and the tribute-fish specimens of the dominion.
Gill: the words far exceed Adam's grant — all power in heaven and earth given to the risen Christ, even the angels among the works under his feet (the Ethiopic 'all the works of thy hands').
Clarke: it could never be said of Adam that ALL things were under his feet; this is literally true only of the Lord Jesus, exalted after emptying himself (Phil. 2:6-9).

debates.question: Whose is the dominion of 'all things under his feet'?

sides.position: the literal man's kingship over the beasts, which Paul then lifts higher
a dominion so total (even over angels) that it can only be Christ's
both — man's by creation, Christ's by right of exaltation

themes: dominion over the works of God's hands

schools.summary: Gill glosses sheep and oxen as the tame creatures, useful for food and clothing, the household wealth nearest man's door.
Clarke sorts the verse into its ranks — domestic animals and beasts of husbandry, then the wild 'beasts of the field.'

Keil and Delitzsch mark the graded enumeration (tame to wild) and the poet's enthusiasm, and lift it to the NT: the title 'Son of Man' leans on this psalm no less than on Dan. 7:13, and Hebrews builds on the dominion (Heb. 2:6-8).
Henry marvels that man masters creatures stronger and swifter than himself — every kind tamed (Jas. 3:7) and used at will ('Rise, Peter, kill and eat,' Acts 10:13).

themes: the Son of Man and Daniel 7:13

schools.summary: Gill recalls how God commands the birds to serve his people (quails, the ravens that fed Elijah) or to punish his enemies.

Clarke grounds the grant in the Noahic covenant (Gen. 9:2) — man's general dominion over fowl and fish still — and records the older spiritualizing of the creatures through Bishop Horne and an ancient Psalter.
Henry dwells on the fish in another element, passing unseen through the paths of the seas, yet mastered by man's arts though stronger and swifter than he.

Ellicott prefers the poetic 'whatsoever passeth,' hears in 'the paths of the seas' an echo of Homer's watery ways, and calls the returning refrain the one deliberate touch of art, binding the poem into a wreath.

outliers.note: Records at length the devotional spiritualizing of the creatures — sheep as the faithful, oxen as Church labourers, wild beasts as tempers subdued, birds and fish as spirits under the King Messiah — traced through Bishop Horne and an ancient Psalter.

themes: fowl of the air and fish of the sea

schools.summary: Gill: the sense the psalmist set out with has only deepened, confirmed by the instances he noticed, so that he closes with the very words he opened.
Keil and Delitzsch: having shown the name glorious on earth as in heaven, the poet repeats his opening thought in a wider meaning and weaves the psalm into a wreath.

Spurgeon: like a good composer the poet returns to his key-note, the opening proposition now a proven conclusion, a quod erat demonstrandum; Henry: the earth honoured with the Redeemer's presence, still enlightened by his gospel.
Clarke gives the refrain gospel breadth — the excellent name is the name of Jesus, carried by Bibles and missionaries to the utmost nations.

themes: the psalm woven into a wreath
the name of Jesus in all the earth
